Press |isbn=978-0-7486-2758-5 |edition=Repr |location=Edinburgh}} is a [[Cariban languages|Cariban language]] spoken by 600 people on the [[Nhamundá River]], a tributary of the [[Amazon River]] in [[Brazil]]. It is one of 17 languages that have [[object–verb–subject]] word order, initially described by linguist [[Desmond C. Derbyshire]].{{Cite journal |last=Kalin |first=Laura |date=November 2014 |title=The syntax of OVS word order in Hixkaryana |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s11049-014-9244-x |journal=Natural Language & Linguistic Theory |language=en |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=1089–1104 |doi=10.1007/s11049-014-9244-x |issn=0167-806X|url-access=subscription }} == History == The Hixkaryana are first recorded under the name "Babui" or "Wabuí" in 1725. A wordlist appearing under this name published in 1947 is essentially identical with modern Hixkaryana. The name "Hixkaryana" was originally the name of one of their clans.{{cite book |author=Derbyshire, D. |title=Hixkaryana and Linguistic Typology |publisher=Summer Institute of Linguistics |year=1985 |isbn=0-88312-082-8 |location=Dallas, TX}} [[Čestmír Loukotka]] (1968) lists both "Hishcariana" and "Uaiboí" in his "Waiwai group" in the Cariban languages.{{Cite book |last=Loukotka|first=Čestmír|url=https://etnolinguistica.wdfiles.com/local--files/biblio%3Aloukotka-1968-classification/Loukotka_1968_ClassSAIndLang_001_278.pdf|title=Classification of South American Indian Languages|date=1968|publisher=Latin American Center, University of California Los Angeles|isbn=9780879031077|editor-last=Wilbert|editor-first=Johannes|edition=4th|location=Latin American Center, UCLA|pages=239|lccn=}} ==Phonology== === Consonants === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" |+Hixkaryana consonants ! colspan="2" | ! Before the close vowel {{IPA|/e/}}, only {{IPA|/𝼈/}} may occur, but in other environments it is contrastive with {{IPA|/ɾ/}}. === Vowels === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" |+ ! ![[Front vowel|Front]] ![[Back vowel|Back]] |- ![[Close vowel|Close]] | |{{IPAlink|ɯ}} {{grapheme|ɨ}}, {{IPAlink|u}} {{grapheme|u}} |- ![[Close-mid vowel|Close-mid]] |{{IPAlink|e}} {{grapheme|e}} | |- ![[Open-mid vowel|Open-mid]] | |{{IPAlink|ɔ}} {{grapheme|o}} |- ![[Open vowel|Open]] |{{IPAlink|æ}} {{grapheme|a}} | |} {{IPA|/e/}} has a number of allophones in certain environment; it is realized as closer {{IPA|[i]}} after a postalveolar consonant, a long {{IPA|[i]}} with a central glide {{IPA|[iːᵊ]}} preceding a syllable with a back vowel, as close, less tense {{IPA|[ɪ]}} in unstressed syllables followed by a syllable which does not have stressed {{IPA|/e/}}, and as {{IPA|[e]}} elsewhere. ==Grammar== In Hixkaryana, arguments are indexed on the verb by personal prefixes, which form an inverse-like pattern in which the argument highest in the hierarchy 2nd > 1st > 3rd is indexed on the verb. If the object of a transitive verb outranks the subject, the appropriate O-prefix is used; otherwise, an A-prefix is used. {| class="wikitable" ! colspan="2" | A-prefixes || colspan="2" | O-prefixes |- ! 1A | 0-/ɨ- ! 1O | r(o) |- ! 2A | m(ɨ)- ! 2O | o(j)-/a(j)- |- ! 1+2A | t(ɨ)- ! 1+2O | k(ɨ)- |- ! 3A | n(ɨ)-/j- |} Intransitive verbs take prefixes mostly similar to the transitive prefixes, with an [[Active–stative alignment|active–stative]]. The arguments' grammatical number is indexed on the verb by portmanteau suffixes that combine tense, aspect, mood, and number. Hixkaryana has an [[object–verb–subject]] word order. In most cases, the person prefixes clearly indicate which arguments are the subject and object. When both the subject and the object are third person, however, the person prefix is inadequate to fully determine the identity of the arguments, requiring word order. The example below, {{lang|hix|toto yonoye kamara}}, cannot be given the AVO reading {{gloss|the man ate the jaguar}}; the OVA reading – {{gloss|the jaguar ate the man}} – is the only possible one. {{interlinear|indent=3 |top= {{lang|hix|toto yonoye kamara}} |toto y- ono -ye kamara |person 3SG- eat -DIST.PAST.COMPL jaguar |{{gloss|The jaguar ate the man.}}|lang=hix}} Indirect objects, however, follow the subject: {{interlinear | indent = 3 | top = {{lang|hix|bɨryekomo yotahahono wosɨ tɨnyo wya}}|bɨryekomo y- otaha -ho -no wosɨ tɨnyo wya|boy 3SG- hit -CAUS -IMM.PAST woman her-husband by|{{gloss|The woman caused her husband to hit the boy.}} | lang = hix }} Moreover, the word order in non-finite [[embedded clause]]s is SOV.{{cite paper |date=2006-07-18 |title=Word Order Variation: The head parameter |url=http://www.ling.umd.edu/~soltan/LING419B/Handouts/handout3.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070221213347/http://www.ling.umd.edu/~soltan/LING419B/Handouts/handout3.pdf |archive-date=2007-02-21 |access-date=2024-12-15 |website=ling.umd.edu}} Like most other languages with objects preceding the verb, it is [[postposition]]al. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Bibliography== * {{cite book | author=Aikhenvald, A. & Dixon, R.
